parts.visual:
A perfectionist engineering team spends 6 months building an incredible, flawless new feature. They launch it. Zero users click on it. They just wasted $500,000 of investor money building something nobody wanted.

The Solution:
1. Shipping Fast: The philosophy that releasing imperfect code quickly is mathematically superior to releasing perfect code slowly.
2. MVF (Minimum Viable Feature): Instead of building the entire feature, you build the ugliest, fastest version of it in 3 days just to see if any users actually click the button.
parts.audio: In a startup, speed is your only defensible advantage against massive corporations. If you are not deeply embarrassed by the first version of your product when you launch it, you launched too late.

questions.question: A Product Manager wants to add an 'Export to PDF' button. The engineers say it will take 3 weeks to build the PDF generator. How can the PM test this as a 'Minimum Viable Feature' in 1 hour?
options: Put a fake 'Export to PDF' button on the site. When users click it, show a pop-up saying 'Coming Soon!' and count how many people clicked it. If nobody clicks, you saved 3 weeks of engineering time.
Build the PDF generator in 3 hours.
questions.correct_answer: Put a fake 'Export to PDF' button on the site. When users click it, show a pop-up saying 'Coming Soon!' and count how many people clicked it. If nobody clicks, you saved 3 weeks of engineering time.
questions.explanation: This is called a 'Painted Door Test'. It measures intent before writing code.

questions.question: Listen to the CEO yelling at the CTO. Why is the CEO angry about the code quality?
questions.tts_text: I don't care if the code is messy! We are a startup, not NASA! If this feature has a few bugs, the users will complain and we will fix it tomorrow. But if we wait another month to launch it perfectly, we will run out of money and die.
options: The trade-off between Quality and Survival. Perfect code is a luxury that early-stage startups cannot afford. The market rewards speed of iteration far more than it rewards initial perfection.
questions.correct_answer: The trade-off between Quality and Survival. Perfect code is a luxury that early-stage startups cannot afford. The market rewards speed of iteration far more than it rewards initial perfection.
questions.explanation: If your product is perfect, you spent too much time building it.

questions.question: What is 'Feature Creep'?
options: A scary person in the office.
The deadly tendency to constantly add new requirements and 'cool ideas' to a project while it is being built, which delays the launch date indefinitely and burns through all the cash.
questions.correct_answer: The deadly tendency to constantly add new requirements and 'cool ideas' to a project while it is being built, which delays the launch date indefinitely and burns through all the cash.
questions.explanation: Feature creep is the enemy of shipping fast. You must lock the scope.

questions.question: Why do elite engineering teams practice 'Continuous Deployment'?
options: It is a system that automatically pushes code to the live servers multiple times a day. Instead of one massive, terrifying 'Launch Day' every 6 months, updates happen instantly and continuously, reducing risk.
questions.correct_answer: It is a system that automatically pushes code to the live servers multiple times a day. Instead of one massive, terrifying 'Launch Day' every 6 months, updates happen instantly and continuously, reducing risk.
questions.explanation: Small, frequent updates are drastically safer than massive, rare updates.

pairs.match: The act of releasing a product or feature to the live market
The ongoing expansion of new features in a product, leading to endless delays
Automated software release process pushing updates multiple times a day
Adding a fake button to test user demand before writing the actual code
